title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 873–874 (Night 206, continuing nights-205), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 206 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Qamar al-Zamān and the Lady Budūr ask King al-Ghayūr's leave to travel to his father; the king lets Budūr go with him for a year, fits them out with horses, camels, a litter, servants and gifts, and at parting embraces his daughter and weeps two lines of verse on farewell. After a month on the road they camp in a wide meadow; Qamar al-Zamān finds Budūr asleep, her thin apricot-coloured shift blown up by the wind, and, stirred, recites two lines of love. Untying the drawstring of her drawers he finds a red stone tied to it, engraved with two lines of names in an unreadable script; wondering why she guards it so closely, he takes it out of the tent to look at it in the light, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and sixth night,
sentences.n: The night is numbered “the sixth after the two hundred”: al-sādisa, “the sixth”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا أَخْبَرَ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ بِمَا رَآهُ فِى النَّوْمِ دَخَلَتْ هِيَ وَإِيَّاهُ عَلَى وَالِدِهَا وَأَعْلَمَاهُ بِذٰلِكَ وَاسْتَأْذَنَاهُ فِى السَّفَرِ فَأَذِنَ لَهُ بِالسَّفَرِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā akhbara al-sitta Budūra bi-mā raʾāhu fī al-nawmi dakhalat hiya wa-iyyāhu ʿalā wālidihā wa-aʿlamāhu bi-dhālika wa-istaʾdhanāhu fī al-safari fa-adhina lahu bi-al-safari
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, when he-informed the-Lady Budūr of-what he-saw-it in the-sleep, went-in she and-him to her-father, and-they-two-informed-him of-that, and-they-two-asked-his-leave for the-journey; and-he-gave-leave to-him for-the-journey.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān had told the Lady Budūr what he had seen in his sleep, she and he went in together to her father, told him of it, and asked his leave to travel; and he gave him leave to go.
sentences.n: al-sitt, “the Lady”, is the colloquial title of a woman of rank, set before her name: al-sitt Budūr. akhbara … bi-, “to inform someone of”: bi-mā, “of what”, and the -hu of raʾāhu returns to mā; the آ of رآه is printed. dakhalat hiya wa-iyyāhu, “she went in, she and him”: Classical would say hiya wa-huwa; joining a second subject with the object pronoun iyyāhu is a Middle Arabic habit, kept here. aʿlamāhu and istaʾdhanāhu are duals, “the two of them informed him … asked his leave”: aʿlama bi-, “to let someone know of”, and istaʾdhana, Form X of adhina, “to ask leave”; the hamza of واستأذناه is printed. adhina li- … bi-, “to give someone leave for”: li- marks the one permitted, bi- the thing permitted. The print spells fī both فى and في; both are kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ يَا وَالِدِي أَنَا لَا أَصْبِرُ عَلَى فِرَاقِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-sittu Budūru yā wālidī anā lā aṣbiru ʿalā firāqihi
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-Lady Budūr: O my-father, I, not I-endure upon his-parting.
sentences.i: Then the Lady Budūr said to him, “Father, I cannot bear to be parted from him.”
sentences.n: ṣabara ʿalā, “to be patient under, to bear”: ʿalā marks what is borne. firāq, “parting, separation”, verbal noun of Form III fāraqa; firāqihi, “parting from him”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا وَالِدُهَا سَافِرِي مَعَهُ وَأَذِنَ لَهَا بِالْإِقَامَةِ مَعَهُ سَنَةً كَامِلَةً وَبَعْدَهَا تَأْتِي لِتَزُورَ وَالِدَهَا فِي كُلِّ عَامٍ مَرَّةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā wāliduhā sāfirī maʿahu wa-adhina lahā bi-al-iqāmati maʿahu sanatan kāmilatan wa-baʿdahā taʾtī li-tazūra wālidahā fī kulli ʿāmin marratan
sentences.l: And-said to-her her-father: Travel (f.) with-him. And-he-gave-leave to-her for-the-staying with-him a-year complete, and-after-it she-comes to-visit her-father in every year once.
sentences.i: Her father said to her, “Travel with him,” and he gave her leave to stay with him a whole year, and after that she was to come and visit her father once every year.
sentences.n: sāfirī, feminine imperative of Form III sāfara, “to travel”. iqāma, “staying, residing”, verbal noun of Form IV aqāma. sanatan kāmilatan, “a full year”, accusative of time. taʾtī li-tazūra, “she comes to visit”: li- with the subjunctive gives purpose; the father's permission is reported in the third person, “she is to come”. The hamza of تأتي is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلَتْ يَدَ أَبِيهَا وَكَذٰلِكَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qabbalat yada abīhā wa-ka-dhālika Qamaru al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-she-kissed (the) hand (of) her-father, and-likewise Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: She kissed her father's hand, and so did Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: abīhā, “her father”: ab takes a long vowel before a suffix, here genitive abī-. ka-dhālika, “like that, likewise”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَرَعَ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ فِي تَجْهِيزِ ابْنَتِهِ وَزَوْجِهَا وَهَيَّأَ لَهُمَا الْمُؤْنَةَ وَأَدَوَاتِ السَّفَرِ
sentences.tr: thumma sharaʿa al-maliku al-Ghayūru fī tajhīzi ibnatihi wa-zawjihā wa-hayyaʾa lahumā al-muʾnata wa-adawāti al-safari
sentences.l: Then began the-king al-Ghayūr in equipping (of) his-daughter and-her-husband, and-he-prepared for-them-two the-provisions and-(the)-implements (of) the-journey.
sentences.i: Then King al-Ghayūr set about fitting out his daughter and her husband, and made ready for them provisions and all the gear of the journey.
sentences.n: sharaʿa fī, “to begin, set about”, with fī before the verbal noun. tajhīz, Form II verbal noun, “equipping, fitting out”, especially for a journey or a bride. muʾna, “provisions, supplies”; the ؤ of المؤنة and the hamza of هيّأ are printed, as is the shadda of هيّأ, Form II hayyaʾa, “to make ready”.

sentences.t: وَأَخْرَجَ لَهُمَا الْخُيُولَ الْمُسَوَّمَةَ وَالْهُجُنَ الْعُشَارِيَّ وَأَخْرَجَ لِابْنَتِهِ مِحَفَّةً وَحَمَّلَ لَهُمَا الْبِغَالَ وَالْهُجُنَ وَاسْتَخْدَمَ لَهُمَا الْعَبِيدَ وَالرِّجَالَ وَأَخْرَجَ لَهُمَا كُلَّمَا يَحْتَاجَانِ إِلَيْهِ فِى السَّفَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhraja lahumā al-khuyūla al-musawwamata wa-al-hujuna al-ʿushāriyya wa-akhraja li-ibnatihi miḥaffatan wa-ḥammala lahumā al-bighāla wa-al-hujuna wa-istakhdama lahumā al-ʿabīda wa-al-rijāla wa-akhraja lahumā kullamā yaḥtājāni ilayhi fī al-safari
sentences.l: And-he-brought-out for-them-two the-horses, the-marked-ones, and-the-dromedaries, the-ʿushārī, and-brought-out for-his-daughter a-litter, and-loaded for-them-two the-mules and-the-dromedaries, and-took-into-service for-them-two the-slaves and-the-men, and-brought-out for-them-two all-that they-two-need of-it in the-journey.
sentences.i: He brought out for them the finest horses and swift dromedaries, brought out a litter for his daughter, loaded mules and camels for them, took slaves and men into service for them, and gave them everything they would need on the journey.
sentences.n: al-khayl al-musawwama, “marked horses”, is an old phrase for horses of the best breeding, turned out to pasture or marked for war. hujun, plural of hajīn, “riding dromedary”. al-ʿushārī is uncertain: Lane gives ʿusharāʾ, “a she-camel ten months pregnant”, prized beasts; here it is more likely a later word for a swift riding camel; the doubled yāʾ is our pointing. miḥaffa, “litter”, a covered seat carried on a camel or between mules; the shadda is printed. ḥammala, Form II, “to load (beasts)”: the print has no marks here, and the Form I reading ḥamala, “carry”, is also possible. istakhdama, Form X of khadama, “to take into service”. The print sets kullamā as one word for kull mā, “all that”, as it often does; it is kept. iḥtāja ilā, “to need”: ilayhi returns to mā. The li- on lahumā throughout marks those the things are for.

sentences.t: وَفِي يَوْمِ الْمَسِيرِ وَدَّعَ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَخَلَعَ عَلَيْهِ عَشْرَ خِلَعٍ سَنِيَّةٍ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ مُرَصَّعَةٍ بِالْجَوَاهِرِ وَقَدَّمَ لَهُ عَشَرَةَ خُيُولٍ وَعَشْرَ نِيَاقٍ وَخَزْنَةَ مَالٍ
sentences.tr: wa-fī yawmi al-masīri waddaʿa al-maliku al-Ghayūru Qamara al-Zamāni wa-khalaʿa ʿalayhi ʿashra khilaʿin saniyyatin mina al-dhahabi muraṣṣaʿatin bi-al-jawāhiri wa-qaddama lahu ʿasharata khuyūlin wa-ʿashra niyāqin wa-khaznata mālin
sentences.l: And-on (the) day (of) the-setting-out, bade-farewell the-king al-Ghayūr (to) Qamar al-Zamān, and-he-put-on him ten robes splendid of the-gold, studded with-the-jewels, and-presented to-him ten horses and-ten she-camels and-a-treasure (of) money.
sentences.i: On the day of departure King al-Ghayūr bade Qamar al-Zamān farewell and invested him with ten splendid robes of gold studded with jewels, and presented him with ten horses, ten she-camels and a treasure-chest of money.
sentences.n: The print sets the shadda of سنيّة on the nūn, سنّية, a misprint for the yāʾ, corrected here. waddaʿa, Form II, “to bid farewell”, takes the person as its object. khalaʿa ʿalā, “to put (a robe of honour) on someone”: khilʿa, plural khilaʿ, is the robe a king bestows. ʿashr khilaʿ and ʿashr niyāq have the short numeral because khilʿa and nāqa are feminine; ʿasharat khuyūl has the long one. saniyya, “splendid, exalted”. muraṣṣaʿ, “inlaid, studded”, Form II passive participle; bi- marks what it is studded with. khazna, “treasury”, here a treasure-load of money, a set amount in this later Arabic.

sentences.t: وَأَوْصَاهُ عَلَى بِنْتِهِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ وَخَرَجَ مَعَهُمَا إِلَى أَقْصَى الْجَزَائِرِ
sentences.tr: wa-awṣāhu ʿalā bintihi al-sitti Budūra wa-kharaja maʿahumā ilā aqṣā al-jazāʾiri
sentences.l: And-he-charged-him upon his-daughter the-Lady Budūr, and-went-out with-them-two to (the) farthest (of) the-Islands.
sentences.i: He commended his daughter the Lady Budūr to his care, and rode out with them to the farthest bounds of the Islands.
sentences.n: awṣā, Form IV, “to charge, enjoin”: Classical says awṣāhu bi-, the text has ʿalā, a later usage. bint, “daughter”, stands here beside the ibna of the sentences around it. al-jazāʾir, “the Islands”: Budūr's father is lord of “the Islands and the Seas”; the ئ is printed. aqṣā, “farthest”, elative of qaṣiya.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ وَدَّعَ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَدَخَلَ عَلَى ابْنَتِهِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ وَهِيَ فِى الْمِحَفَّةِ وَضَمَّهَا وَقَبَّلَهَا وَصَارَ يَبْكِي وَيَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma waddaʿa Qamara al-Zamāni wa-dakhala ʿalā ibnatihi al-sitti Budūra wa-hiya fī al-miḥaffati wa-ḍammahā wa-qabbalahā wa-ṣāra yabkī wa-yaqūlu
sentences.l: Then he-bade-farewell (to) Qamar al-Zamān and-went-in to his-daughter the-Lady Budūr, and-she (was) in the-litter, and-he-embraced-her and-kissed-her and-he-began weeping and-saying:
sentences.i: Then he bade Qamar al-Zamān farewell and went in to his daughter the Lady Budūr where she sat in her litter, held her close and kissed her, and began to weep, saying:
sentences.n: wa-hiya fī al-miḥaffa, “and she in the litter”: a circumstantial clause with wa-. ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin to do”: ṣāra yabkī wa-yaqūlu, “he began weeping and saying”.

sentences.t:
يَا طَالِبًا لِلْفِرَاقِ مَهْلًا * فَمُتْعَةُ الْعَاشِقِ الْعِنَاقُ
مَهْلًا فَطَبْعُ الزَّمَان غَدْرٌ * وَآخِرُ الْعَشْرَةِ الْفِرَاقُ
sentences.tr:
yā ṭāliban li-al-firāqi mahlan * fa-mutʿatu al-ʿāshiqi al-ʿināqu
mahlan fa-ṭabʿu al-zamān ghadrun * wa-ākhiru al-ʿashrati al-firāqu
sentences.l:
O seeker for the-parting, gently! * For (the) delight (of) the-lover (is) the-embrace.
Gently! For (the) nature (of) the-time (is) treachery, * and-(the)-end (of) the-companionship (is) the-parting.
sentences.i:
You who are so eager to part, go gently: * the lover's whole delight is to embrace.
Go gently: treachery is time's nature, * and every fellowship must end in parting.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on al-ʿināq / al-firāq. yā ṭāliban, “O one seeking”: the vocative of an indefinite, unnamed person takes the accusative. mahlan, “gently, slowly!”, an accusative used as an exclamation. ʿināq, “embracing”, verbal noun of Form III ʿānaqa. The print leaves the final vowel off الزَّمَان, kept so. It points الْعَشْرَةِ, al-ʿashra, “the ten”; the sense wants al-ʿishra, “companionship”, the same letters; the print's pointing is kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَ مِنْ عِنْدِ ابْنَتِهِ وَأَتَى إِلَى زَوْجِهَا قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فَصَارَ يُوَدِّعُهُ وَيُقَبِّلُهُ ثُمَّ فَارَقَهُمَا وَرَجَعَ إِلَى مَمْلَكَتِهِ بِعَسْكَرِهِ بَعْدَ أَنْ أَمَرَهُمَا بِالرَّحِيلِ
sentences.tr: thumma kharaja min ʿindi ibnatihi wa-atā ilā zawjihā Qamari al-Zamāni fa-ṣāra yuwaddiʿuhu wa-yuqabbiluhu thumma fāraqahumā wa-rajaʿa ilā mamlakatihi bi-ʿaskarihi baʿda an amarahumā bi-al-raḥīli
sentences.l: Then he-went-out from (the) presence (of) his-daughter and-came to her-husband Qamar al-Zamān, and-he-began bidding-him-farewell and-kissing-him; then he-parted-from-them-two and-returned to his-kingdom with-his-army, after that he-commanded-them-two with-the-departure.
sentences.i: Then he came away from his daughter and went to her husband Qamar al-Zamān, and bade him farewell and kissed him; then he left them and returned to his kingdom with his troops, after bidding them set out.
sentences.n: min ʿindi, “from beside, from the presence of”. bi-ʿaskarihi: bi- of accompaniment, “with his army”. amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes bi- for the thing commanded, here raḥīl, “departure”.

sentences.t: فَسَارَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَزَوْجَتُهُ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ وَمَنْ مَعَهُمْ مِنَ الْأَتْبَاعِ أَوَّلَ يَوْمٍ وَالثَّانِيَ وَالثَّالِثَ وَالرَّابِعَ
sentences.tr: fa-sāra Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-zawjatuhu al-sittu Budūru wa-man maʿahum mina al-atbāʿi awwala yawmin wa-al-thāniya wa-al-thālitha wa-al-rābiʿa
sentences.l: And-journeyed Qamar al-Zamān and-his-wife the-Lady Budūr and-whoever (was) with-them of the-followers, (the) first day, and-the-second, and-the-third, and-the-fourth,
sentences.i: So Qamar al-Zamān set out with his wife the Lady Budūr and their retinue, and travelled the first day, and the second, the third and the fourth;
sentences.n: zawja, “wife”: Classical prefers zawj for both spouses; the text uses both zawj, “husband”, and zawja. atbāʿ, “followers, retinue”, plural of tabaʿ. awwala yawmin and the ordinals after it are accusatives of time.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا مُسَافِرِينَ مُدَّةَ شَهْرٍ كَامِلٍ فَنَزَلُوا فِي مَرْجٍ وَاسِعِ الْفَلَا كَثِيرِ الْكَلَاءِ وَضَرَبُوا خِيَامَهُمْ فِيهِ وَأَكَلُوا وَشَرِبُوا وَاسْتَرَاحُوا
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū musāfirīna muddata shahrin kāmilin fa-nazalū fī marjin wāsiʿi al-falā kathīri al-kalāʾi wa-ḍarabū khiyāmahum fīhi wa-akalū wa-sharibū wa-istarāḥū
sentences.l: and-not they-ceased travelling (for the) space (of) a-month complete; then-they-alighted in a-meadow wide (of) the-open-land, abundant (of) the-pasture, and-they-struck their-tents in-it, and-ate and-drank and-rested.
sentences.i: and they went on travelling for a whole month, until they halted in a meadow of wide open country and rich pasture, pitched their tents there, ate and drank and rested.
sentences.n: lam yazālū, “they did not cease”, with a predicate in the accusative: “they kept on travelling”. wāsiʿ al-falā, kathīr al-kalāʾ, “wide of open land, abundant of herbage”: adjectives in construct with the thing they describe, a rhyming pair. falā, “open desert, waste”. kalaʾ, “fresh herbage, pasture”, is spelt here الكلاء, with a long ā before the hamza; it is kept as printed and pointed al-kalāʾ. ḍaraba khayma, “to strike a tent”, that is, to pitch it.

sentences.t: وَنَامَتِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ فَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ فَوَجَدَهَا نَائِمَةً
sentences.tr: wa-nāmati al-sittu Budūru fa-dakhala ʿalayhā Qamaru al-Zamāni fa-wajadahā nāʾimatan
sentences.l: And-slept the-Lady Budūr; and-went-in upon-her Qamar al-Zamān and-found-her sleeping.
sentences.i: The Lady Budūr fell asleep, and Qamar al-Zamān went in to her and found her sleeping.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (someone)”. The ئ of نائمة is printed; nāʾimatan, accusative, says how he found her.

sentences.t: وَفَوْقَ بَدَنِهَا قَمِيصٌ مِشْمِشِيٌّ مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ يَبِينُ مِنْهُ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ وَفَوْقَ رَأْسِهَا كُوفِيَّةٌ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ مُرَصَّعَةٌ بِالدُّرِّ وَالْجَوَاهِرِ
sentences.tr: wa-fawqa badanihā qamīṣun mishmishiyyun mina al-ḥarīri yabīnu minhu kullu shayʾin wa-fawqa raʾsihā kūfiyyatun mina al-dhahabi muraṣṣaʿatun bi-al-durri wa-al-jawāhiri
sentences.l: And-over her-body (was) a-shift apricot(-coloured) of the-silk, shows through-it every thing; and-over her-head a-cap of the-gold, studded with-the-pearls and-the-jewels.
sentences.i: Over her body was a shift of apricot-coloured silk through which everything showed, and on her head a cap of gold studded with pearls and jewels.
sentences.n: qamīṣ, “shift, chemise”, the long shirt worn next to the skin. mishmishī, “apricot-coloured”, from mishmish, “apricot”. yabīnu minhu kullu shayʾ, “everything shows through it”: the silk is sheer. kūfiyya, a cap or head-cloth. durr, “pearls”, collective. The ء of شيء and the hamza of رأسها are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ رَفَعَ الْهَوَاءُ قَمِيصَهَا فَطَلَعَ فَوْقَ سُرَّتِهَا وَبَانَتْ نُهُودُهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad rafaʿa al-hawāʾu qamīṣahā fa-ṭalaʿa fawqa surratihā wa-bānat nuhūduhā
sentences.l: And-already had-lifted the-air her-shift, and-it-rose above her-navel, and-showed her-breasts.
sentences.i: The breeze had lifted her shift so that it had ridden up above her navel, and her breasts were bare.
sentences.n: wa-qad with the perfect describes what had already happened: the scene as he finds it. hawāʾ, “air”, and so “breeze, wind”. ṭalaʿa, “to rise, come up”. nuhūd, plural of nahd, “breast”; bāna, “to appear, show”.

sentences.t: وَظَهَرَ لَهَا بَطْنٌ أَبْيَضُ مِنَ الثَّلْجِ وَكُلُّ عُكْنَةٍ مِنْ عُكَنِ طَيَّاتِهِ تَسَعُ أُوقِيَّةً مِنْ دُهْنِ الْبَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ẓahara lahā baṭnun abyaḍu mina al-thalji wa-kullu ʿuknatin min ʿukani ṭayyātihi tasaʿu ūqiyyatan min duhni al-bāni
sentences.l: And-appeared of-her a-belly whiter than the-snow, and-every fold of (the) folds (of) its-creases would-hold an-ounce of oil (of) the-ben.
sentences.i: And there showed a belly of hers whiter than snow, each of whose soft folds could hold an ounce of oil of ben.
sentences.n: ẓahara lahā, “there appeared, belonging to her”: li- marks whose belly it is. abyaḍu min, “whiter than”: the colour adjective serves as a comparative. ʿukna, plural ʿukan, “a fold of fat on the belly”, a mark of beauty in this poetry; ṭayyāt, “folds, creases”. tasaʿu, “it holds, has room for”, from wasiʿa; the fatḥa on the tāʾ and the ḍamma on the ʿayn are printed. ūqiyya, “ounce”. duhn al-bān, the scented oil of the ben tree, the bān whose slender boughs the poets compare to a woman's figure.

sentences.t: فَزَادَ مَحَبَّةً وَهُيَامًا وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-zāda maḥabbatan wa-huyāman wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And-he-increased (in) love and-love-madness, and-he-recited saying:
sentences.i: His love and longing grew the more, and he recited:
sentences.n: zāda, “to increase”, with the accusatives maḥabbatan wa-huyāman saying in what: “he grew in love and passion”. huyām, “love-madness”, the thirst and wandering of a lover. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the usual lead into verse.

sentences.t:
لَوْ قِيلَ لِي وَزَفِيرُ الْحَرِّ يَتَّقِدُ * وَالنَّارُ فِي الْقَلْبِ وَالْاَحْشَاءِ تَضْطَرِمُ
اَهُمْ تُرِيدُ وَتَهْوَى اَنْ تُشَاهِدَهُمْ * اَوْ شَرْبَةً مِنْ زُلَالِ الْمَاءِ قُلْتُ هُمُ
sentences.tr:
law qīla lī wa-zafīru al-ḥarri yattaqidu * wa-al-nāru fī al-qalbi wa-al-aḥshāʾi taḍṭarimu
ahum turīdu wa-tahwā an tushāhidahum * aw sharbatan min zulāli al-māʾi qultu humu
sentences.l:
If it-were-said to-me, while-(the)-sighing (of) the-heat blazes * and-the-fire in the-heart and-the-entrails flares:
“Is-it-them you-want and-long that you-behold-them, * or a-draught of (the) cool-pure (of) the-water?” I-would-say: “Them.”
sentences.i:
If, while my burning sighs blaze up * and fire flares in my heart and in my breast,
I were asked, “Is it they you long to see, * or a draught of cool, clear water?”, I would answer, “They.”
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on taḍṭarimu / humu. zafīr, “a deep sigh, the drawing in of breath”. iḍṭarama, Form VIII, “to blaze, flare”. aḥshāʾ, “the inward parts”, the seat of passion. a-hum, the question prefix a- on hum: “is it they?”. The beloved is spoken of in the plural, as Arabic love poetry often does. zulāl, “cool, sweet, clear (water)”. law … qultu, “if … I would say”: the perfect serves for the unreal condition. The print sets a bare alif on اَهُمْ, اَنْ, اَوْ, الْاَحْشَاءِ without the hamza; it is kept.

sentences.t: فَحَطَّ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَدَهُ فِي دِكَّةِ لِبَاسِهَا فَجَذَبَهَا وَحَلَّهَا لَمَّا اشْتَهَاهَا خَاطِرُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥaṭṭa Qamaru al-Zamāni yadahu fī dikkati libāsihā fa-jadhabahā wa-ḥallahā lammā ishtahāhā khāṭiruhu
sentences.l: And-put Qamar al-Zamān his-hand on (the) drawstring (of) her-drawers, and-he-pulled-it and-undid-it, when desired-her his-heart.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān put his hand to the drawstring of her drawers, pulled it and undid it, for his heart desired her.
sentences.n: ḥaṭṭa, “to put down”, in later Arabic simply “to put, place”. dikka, “the drawstring or waistband of the drawers”; libās here, as often in the Nights, means the drawers, sirwāl, not clothing in general. lammā here follows its main clause and gives the reason: “as, since”. khāṭir, “mind, heart”, the seat of wishes: ishtahāhā khāṭiruhu, “his heart desired her”. The shaddas of فحطّ and حلّها are printed.

sentences.t: فَرَأَى فِيهَا فَصًّا أَحْمَرَ مِثْلَ الْعَنْدَمِ مَرْبُوطًا عَلَى دِكَّتِهَا فَحَلَّهُ وَنَظَرَ فِيهِ فَرَأَى عَلَيْهِ أَسْمَاءً مَنْقُوشَةً سَطْرَيْنِ بِكِتَابَةٍ لَا تُقْرَأُ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾā fīhā faṣṣan aḥmara mithla al-ʿandami marbūṭan ʿalā dikkatihā fa-ḥallahu wa-naẓara fīhi fa-raʾā ʿalayhi asmāʾan manqūshatan saṭrayni bi-kitābatin lā tuqraʾu
sentences.l: And-he-saw in-it a-stone red like the-ʿandam, tied on her-drawstring, and-he-untied-it and-looked into-it, and-saw on-it names engraved (in) two-lines in-a-writing (that) not is-read.
sentences.i: There he saw a red stone like dragon's blood, tied to the drawstring; he untied it and looked at it, and saw engraved on it names in two lines, in a script that could not be read.
sentences.n: faṣṣ, “the stone of a ring, a gem”. aḥmar, “red”, takes no tanwīn. ʿandam, “dragon's blood”, the red resin, or the red dye-wood called baqqam; the poets use it for anything deep red. marbūṭan, “tied”, a circumstantial accusative. saṭrayni, “in two lines”, accusative dual. bi-kitābatin: bi- of means, “in a script”; lā tuqraʾu, “that cannot be read”, passive, an unmarked relative clause after an indefinite noun. The hamza of فرأى and of تقرأ is printed.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَوْلَا أَنَّ هٰذَا الْفَصَّ أَمْرٌ عَظِيمٌ عِنْدَهَا مَا رَبَطَتْهُ هٰذِهِ الرَّبْطَةَ عَلَى دِكَّةِ لِبَاسِهَا وَمَا خَبَأَتْهُ فِي أَعَزِّ مَكَانٍ عِنْدَهَا حَتَّى لَا تُفَارِقَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-qāla fī nafsihi lawlā anna hādhā al-faṣṣa amrun ʿaẓīmun ʿindahā mā rabaṭathu hādhihi al-rabṭata ʿalā dikkati libāsihā wa-mā khabaʾathu fī aʿazzi makānin ʿindahā ḥattā lā tufāriqahu
sentences.l: And-wondered Qamar al-Zamān, and-said in himself: Were-it-not that this the-stone (is) a-matter great with-her, not she-would-have-tied-it this the-tying on (the) drawstring (of) her-drawers, and-not she-would-have-hidden-it in (the) dearest place with-her, so-that not she-parts-from-it.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān wondered at it, and said to himself, “If this stone did not matter greatly to her, she would never have tied it like this to the drawstring of her drawers, nor hidden it in the most precious place she has, so as never to be parted from it.
sentences.n: fī nafsihi, “in himself”, that is, to himself. lawlā anna …, “were it not that …”, answered by mā with the perfect: “she would not have …”. rabaṭathu hādhihi al-rabṭata, “she tied it this tying”: the verbal noun of the same verb, as an inner object, gives the manner. The hamza of خبأته is printed; khabaʾa, “to hide”. aʿazz, “dearest, most precious”, elative of ʿazīz. ḥattā lā tufāriqahu, “so that she would not part from it”: ḥattā with the subjunctive gives purpose.

sentences.t: فَيَاتُرَى مَا ذَا تَصْنَعُ بِهٰذَا وَمَا السِّرُّ الَّذِي هُوَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-yā turā mā dhā taṣnaʿu bi-hādhā wa-mā al-sirru alladhī huwa fīhi
sentences.l: And-O will-it-be-seen, what (is) that she-does with-this, and-what (is) the-secret which it (is) in-it?
sentences.i: I wonder, what can she do with it, and what is the secret it holds?”
sentences.n: yā turā, “I wonder”, literally “O, is it seen?”: a later Arabic phrase of musing, here run together as the print sets it, فياترى. The print also sets mā dhā, “what?”, as two words; both are kept. ṣanaʿa bi-, “to do with”: bi- marks the thing dealt with. The shadda of السرّ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَهُ وَخَرَجَ مِنَ الْخَيْمَةِ لِيُبْصِرَهُ فِى النُّورِ
sentences.tr: thumma akhadhahu wa-kharaja mina al-khaymati li-yubṣirahu fī al-nūri
sentences.l: Then he-took-it and-went-out from the-tent to-see-it in the-light.
sentences.i: Then he took it and went out of the tent to look at it in the light.
sentences.n: li-yubṣirahu, “in order to see it”: li- with the subjunctive gives purpose; abṣara, Form IV, “to see, look at closely”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print splits the name here, شهر زاد; it is kept as set.
